latin.49: Praeter aberrationem ab argumento sunt alia vitia in responsionibus tribus D. G. quae paucis indicabo. 1. Nos, inquit, pertendimus certam fuisse causam, quare de imputatione illa loqueretur Apostolus. Nam cum dixisset, unius hominis peccato mortem fuisse introductam in mundum, quaeri potuit, unde ea vis illi peccato, ut tantum mali non in unum aut alterum, sed in omnes invexerit: Respondet Paulus, illud inde factum, quod uno illo peccato omnes rei facti sint, sive quod uno illo peccante omnes in illo et cum illo peccavisse intelligendi sunt. Haec responsio, praeter quam quod non tangit nervum argumenti, Apostolum facit nugantem, et mutatis tantum verbis idipsum quod quaerebatur respondentem, ac pro causa effectus ipsum effectum, cujus causa quaerebatur, afferentem. Quid enim est hujus responsionis autori, peccatum in mundum introiisse? nihil, nisi peccatum actuale omnibus hominibus imputatum fuisse. Id patet clarissime ex hoc ipso ejus cap. 8. §. 8. p. 217. et aliis aliquot locis. Quid rursus ei est in Adamo omnes peccavisse? id sane, inquit, melius exponi non potest, quam si dicamus peccatum Adae omnibus imputari. eodem cap. §. 10. p. 222. Quaerenti ergo cur peccatum actuale Adami omnibus imputetur ad mortem, Responderit Apostolus, quia omnibus imputatur. Quaerenti, unde ea vis illi peccato, ut imputetur non uni aut alteri, sed omnibus, respondet illud inde factum, quod illud imputetur omnibus. Quid est nugari, si hoc non est?
latin.50: Ad duo ista vitia accedit etiam tertium. Sibi enim ipse repugnat. Nam si ea fuit mens Apostoli quam ei tribuit haec responsio, certe verba ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον construi debent, post antecedentia omnia, peccatum in mundum introiit, et per peccatum mors, et ita mors in omnes pervasit: responsio enim essent ad quaestionem, quae ex verbis illis immediate praecedentibus exoriri poterat. Id quod versionem in quo evertit. Ea enim posita construi debent verba in quo omnes peccaverunt, ante illa omnia: cohaerent enim immediate cum nomine ἀνθρώπου et est trajectio. Sic ergo construi deberent, Sicut per unum hominem, in quo omnes peccaverunt, peccatum in mundum introiit, et per peccatum mors, et ita in omnes homines mors pervasit.
latin.51: Secunda similiter responsio peccat ignoratione argumenti, causamque incertam aliter quam debuit accipit, et praeterea nonnulla habet minus recte dicta. Quis dixerit, inquit, incertam causam a Paulo proponi cum I. Cor. xv. 22. ad Adamum usque protoplastam conscendit, et nos omnes dicit in Adamo mori? Quorsum hoc spectat? Ibine causam aliquam affert Apostolus, cur omnes vi communionis quam habent cum Adamo moriantur? aut suntne illa verba, in Adamo omnes moriuntur, etiam imputative, ut loquuntur, intelligenda? Deteriora sunt quae sequuntur. Nimirum, inquit, neque ibi, neque hic Apostolus proprie ad causas particulares respicit, quae residere possunt in unoquoque individuo generis humani, et propter quas fit ut moriantur: sed causam generalem exponit quae omnes in genere ex aequo respiciat etc. Perinde loquitur, quasi corruptio haereditaria non esset causa generalis omnes homines ex aequo respiciens: Cum illa tamen tam sit communis, quam communis est eorum qui peccaverunt mors, quam communis est illis natura humana, immo quam communis dicitur esse imputatio. Ita paulatim doctrina de corruptionis haereditariae vi et reatu, quam summo studio primi reformatores tuebantur, negligitur ac prope obliteratur, ut det locum illi imputationi, quam magni illi viri, aut ignorarunt prorsus, aut etiam refutarunt.
latin.52: Neque par est, addit, ut eam causam dicamus esse remotam et longinquam, quia hic non ad annorum et saeculorum spatia, sed ad rei efficacitatem respiciendum est. Quid? an injustitia, quae in me non haesit, sed in solo Adamo, tot annorum millibus antequam essem mortuo, causa est aeque immediata ac proxima mihi vel morti meae, ac illa quae in me haeret intime, et est omnium confessione mortis meae causa? Annon etiam peccatum Adami secuta est corruptio, et hanc mors? est igitur corruptio causa propinquior mortis quam peccatum quod in solo haesit Adamo. Neque vero, subjungit, qui corruptionem ab Adamo derivari dicunt, Adamum ideo proponunt, tanquam causam remotam et distantem corruptionis illius, nimirum, quia est nobis cum eo ratione sanguinis proxima unio, etsi non ratione personae. Immo eum proponunt, tanquam causam corruptionis illius remotam et distantem, hoc est, primam, unde ad alios omnes dimanavit. Itaque quod sanguis hic a persona distinguitur, et illius, non hujus, ratione nobis esse dicitur proxima cum Adamo unio, id equidem non intelligo. Tam enim sanguis meus a sanguine, et natura mea a natura, quam persona a persona Adami differt: differentia est utriusque pariter numerica, non specifica: Et quam personam meam, tam naturam etiam meam per omnes meos intermedios parentes ab Adamo traxi. Est enim Adamus pater noster non proximus, sed primus; nihilque ab eo nisi per proximos meos parentes, accepi, aut accipere potui.
latin.53: Sed, inquit, cum hic instituatur inter Christum et Adamum comparatio, non magis dicendum est inobedientiam ab Adamo commissam, esse causam remotam nostrae condemnationis, quam obedientiam a Christo praestitam, esse causam remotam nostrae justificationis. Quasi vero non possit comparatio inter duas causas effectuum oppositorum institui, cum sunt in suo genere primae, nisi utraque sit pariter proxima! Quis nescit obedientiam Christi esse justificationis nostrae causam adaequatam et unicam, inobedientiam vero Adami condemnationis nostrae nonnisi inadaequatam et partialem? damnamur enim non ob solum peccatum actuale Adami, sed etiam ob inhaerentem nobis corruptionem haereditariam, et alia omnia nostra peccata sive actualia sive habitualia; cum tamen ob unam Christi obedientiam, nullo autem modo ob nostram, justificemur. Haec igitur, cum sola et unica justificationis causa sit, eadem et prima et proxima est; illa vero cum non sola sit, sed una cum ea aliae multae sint causae condemnationis, ita prima est, ut nihil necesse sit proximam esse. Quid? nonne peccatum et per peccatum condemnationem trahimus ab Adamo propagatione naturali? Nonne et Patres olim, et primi nostri Reformatores imitationi Pelagianae opponere solebant propagationem peccati, nulla imputationis facta mentione? Atqui propagationis naturalis, in suo quidem genere, prima est causa Adamus, sed cujusque nostrum proxima aut immediata profecto non est. Hic ergo maximum cernitur Adamum inter et Christum discrimen. Adamus est generationis nostrae causa remotissima, cum regenerationis nostrae Christus sit causa proxima. Filii sumus Adami non proximi sed remoti: inter nos enim et Adamum alii multi interjecti sunt; Filii vero Christi proximi sumus, quotquot in eum credimus. Per fidem enim unimur Christo recta et immediate, necnon per ejus Spiritum, qui cum unus tantum numero sit et in Christo et in omnibus nobis, nos Christo tam immediate copulat, ut inter Christum et fidelem intermedius nemo sit. Haec cum non ignoraret Vir Doctus, qui potuit sic loqui? Denique in causis meritoriis, inquit, quales sunt de quibus agimus, semper est proximitas, quia meritum illud semper ἐγγύς et efficaciter agit. Egregium argumentum! quasi non possit pariter efficacia, ac causa, distingui in remotam et proximam! sua enim cuique causae vis et, cum sequitur effectum, efficacia est; alioqui non esset causa. Annon Adamus efficaciter naturam suam et corruptionem in nos propagavit? Attamen naturae et corruptionis nostrae causa non est nisi remota. Non est autem ipse causa meritoria condemnationis nostrae, sed hujus causa causae; manavit enim ab eo corruptio haereditaria nostrae condemnationis causa proxima seu immediata, hujus autem causa fuit peccatum actuale Adami. Possumusne similiter dicere, obedientiam Christi causam fuisse alicujus virtutis vel obedientiae, quae sit causa justificationis nostrae? Eatenus igitur inter Christi obedientiam et Adami inobedientiam discrimen est memorabile, et illa proxima justificationis, haec remota condemnationis nostrae (corruptio enim interponitur) causa dicenda est. Alioqui quomodo peccatum actuale Adami causa esse posset condemnationis nostrae meritoria et proxima? Primum si non est nostrum nisi per imputationem, non meretur condemnationem nostram nisi imputationis interventu. Non est igitur causa meritoria nostrae condemnationis per se, sed per accidens tantum, ratione illius imputationis, quae est actio divina, atque adeo supernaturalis et voluntaria: cum tamen obedientia Christi sit causa meritoria justificationis nostrae per se; quippe, eo fine ac consilio a vade nostro loco nostro praestita. Quo posito sequitur, quod sumus peccatores et condemnamur, id esse divinae illi actioni per se ascribendum, peccato vero Adami nonnisi per accidens, id quod ut credam vel faciam adduci me mea nullo modo patitur conscientia. Deinde qui imputat alicui homini peccatum, supponit illum hominem esse, qui damnat ad mortem supponit eum quem damnat vivere. Cum ergo nostri esse et vivere, quod natura condemnationem nostram antecedit, non sit Adamus causa nisi remota, qui potest esse condemnationis nostrae causa proxima?

pass_a.49: Praeter aberrationem ab argumento: alia vitia in responsionibus tribus D. Garissoles, paucis indicabo. (1) Nos pertendimus certam fuisse causam quare Apostolus de imputatione loqueretur. Cum dixisset unius hominis peccato mortem introductam in mundum, quaeri potuit unde ea vis illi peccato ut tantum mali in omnes invexerit non in unum/alteram. Respondet Paulus: inde factum quod uno illo peccato omnes rei facti sint / uno illo peccante omnes in illo et cum illo peccavisse intelligendi. Haec responsio non tangit nervum argumenti; Apostolum facit nugantem; mutatis verbis respondet idipsum quaesitum; pro causa effectus affert ipsum effectum. Autori responsionis: peccatum in mundum introiisse = nihil nisi peccatum actuale omnibus imputatum (cap. 8 §.8 p.217). In Adamo omnes peccavisse = melius = peccatum Adae omnibus imputari (§.10 p.222). Quaerenti cur actuale Adami omnibus imputetur ad mortem → Respondet: quia omnibus imputatur. Quaerenti unde vis ut imputetur omnibus → respondet: quia imputetur omnibus. = nugari.
pass_a.50: Ad duo ista vitia accedit tertium: sibi ipse repugnat. Si mens Apostoli = haec responsio, verba ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον construi debent post antecedentia omnia (peccatum introiit / per peccatum mors / mors in omnes pervasit) — responsio ad quaestionem ex verbis immediate praecedentibus. Id evertit versionem in quo. Ea posita, in quo omnes peccaverunt construi debent ante illa omnia: cohaerent immediate cum ἀνθρώπου; est trajectio. Sic: Sicut per unum hominem, in quo omnes peccaverunt, peccatum introiit… mors pervasit.
pass_a.51: Secunda responsio similiter peccat ignoratione argumenti; causam incertam aliter accipit; nonnulla minus recte dicta. Garissoles: Quis dixerit incertam causam a Paulo proponi cum 1 Cor 15:22 ad Adamum protoplastam conscendit et dicit nos in Adamo mori? Quorsum? Affertne causam cur omnes vi communionis cum Adamo moriantur? An in Adamo omnes moriuntur etiam imputative intelligenda? Deteriora sequuntur: neque ibi neque hic Apostolus ad causas particulares in individuo respicit, sed causam generalem omnes ex aequo. Perinde quasi corruptio haereditaria non esset causa generalis — cum tam communis sit quam mors peccantium / natura humana / imputatio. Ita doctrina de vi et reatu corruptionis haereditariae (primi reformatores summo studio tuebantur) negligitur ac prope obliteratur ut det locum imputationi quam magni viri ignorarunt prorsus aut refutarunt.
pass_a.52: Neque par est (addit) ut eam causam dicamus remotam/longinquam, quia hic non ad annorum/saeculorum spatia sed ad rei efficacitatem respiciendum. Quid? an injustitia in solo Adamo (non in me haesit), tot millibus annorum antequam essem mortuo, causa aeque immediata/proxima mihi/morti meae ac illa quae in me haeret intime et omnium confessione mortis meae causa? Annon peccatum Adami → corruptio → mors; ergo corruptio propinquior quam peccatum in solo Adamo. Qui corruptionem ab Adamo derivari dicunt non proponunt Adamum tanquam remotam quia sanguinis unio proxima (etsi non personae) — Immo proponunt remotam/distantem = primam unde dimanavit. Sanguis a persona distinctus → proxima unio ratione sanguinis non personae: non intelligo. Sanguis/natura mea a Adami differunt numerice non specificae sicut persona. Quam personam, tam naturam traxi per intermedios parentes. Adamus pater non proximus sed primus; nihil nisi per proximos parentes accepi.
pass_a.53: Garissoles: cum instituatur comparatio Christus/Adam, non magis inobedientia Adami causa remota condemnationis quam obedientia Christi causa remota justificationis. Quasi comparatio causarum effectuum oppositorum (primae in genere) exigat utramque pariter proximam! Obedientia Christi = causa adaequata/unica justificationis; inobedientia Adami = inadaequata/partialis condemnationis. Damnamur non ob solum actuale Adami sed ob corruptionem haereditariam + alia peccata; justificamur ob unam Christi obedientiam non nostram. Haec (unica) = prima et proxima; illa (non sola) ita prima ut non necesse proximam. Peccatum/condemnationem trahimus propagatione naturali. Patres + primi Reformatores opponebant propagationem imitationi Pelagianae, nulla imputationis mentione. Propagatio: Adamus prima in genere, sed cujusque proxima/immediata non est. Maximum discrimen: Adamus causa remotissima generationis; Christus causa proxima regenerationis. Filii Adami remoti (multi interjecti); filii Christi proximi per fidem + Spiritum (unus numero) — nullus intermedius. Vir Doctus ignorabat? Denique in causis meritoriis semper proximitas quia meritum semper ἐγγύς et efficaciter agit. Quasi efficacia/causa non distinguantur remota/proxima! Sua vis cuique = efficacia cum sequitur effectum. Adamus efficaciter propagavit naturam/corruptionem, tamen causa remota. Ipse non causa meritoria condemnationis sed causa causae; corruptio haereditaria = causa proxima; hujus causa = actuale Adami. Possumusne dicere obedientiam Christi causam alicujus virtutis quae justificet? Discrimen memorabile: illa proxima justificationis, haec remota condemnationis (corruptio interponitur). Alioqui quomodo actuale Adami meritoria et proxima? Si nostrum nisi per imputationem, non meretur nisi imputationis interventu → causa meritoria per accidens (actio divina supernaturalis/voluntaria), cum obedientia Christi per se (a vade nostro loco nostro). Ergo peccatores/condemnatio ascribenda actioni divinae per se, peccato Adami per accidens — conscientia non patitur. Qui imputat supponit hominem esse; qui damnat ad mortem supponit vivere. Nostri esse/vivere (natura antecedit condemnationem): Adamus causa remota → quomodo causa proxima condemnationis?

49: Besides the aberration from the argument there are other vices in the three responses of D. Garissoles, which I will point out in a few words. 1. "We," he says, "contend that there was a certain cause why the Apostle should speak of that imputation. For when he had said that by one man's sin death was brought into the world (Romans 5:12), it could be asked whence that force to that sin, that it brought so great an evil not upon one or another but upon all: Paul answers that it came about thence, that by that one sin all were made liable, or that that one sinning, all are to be understood to have sinned in him and with him." This response, besides that it does not touch the nerve of the argument, makes the Apostle trifling, and answering, with only the words changed, the very thing that was being asked, and bringing forward as the cause of the effect the effect itself whose cause was being sought. For what is it, to the author of this response, that sin entered into the world? nothing, except that actual sin was imputed to all men. That is clearest from this very chapter 8, §. 8, p. 217 of his, and from some other places. What again is it to him that all sinned in Adam? that, he says, can certainly not be better expounded than if we say that Adam's sin is imputed to all — the same chapter, §. 10, p. 222. To one asking, therefore, why Adam's actual sin is imputed to all unto death, the Apostle will have answered: because it is imputed to all. To one asking whence that force to that sin, that it is imputed not to one or another but to all, he answers that it came about thence, that it is imputed to all. What is it to trifle, if this is not?
50: To those two vices a third also is added. For he contradicts himself. For if that was the mind of the Apostle which this response attributes to him, certainly the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον (Romans 5:12) ought to be construed after all the antecedents — "sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death pervaded into all" — for they would be a response to the question that could arise from those immediately preceding words. That overturns the version "in which." For with that version posited, the words "in which all sinned" ought to be construed before all those: for they cohere immediately with the noun ἀνθρώπου, and there is a transposition. So they ought to be construed: "As through one man, in whom all sinned, sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death pervaded into all men" (Romans 5:12).
51: The second response likewise sins by ignorance of the argument, and takes the uncertain cause otherwise than it ought, and besides has some things less rightly said. "Who will have said," he says, "that an uncertain cause is proposed by Paul, when in 1 Corinthians 15:22 he ascends as far as Adam the first-formed, and says that we all die in Adam?" What does this look to? Does the Apostle there bring forward some cause why all die by the force of the communion they have with Adam? Or are those words, "in Adam all die" (1 Corinthians 15:22), to be understood even imputatively, as they speak? Worse are the things that follow. "Namely," he says, "neither there nor here does the Apostle properly look to particular causes that can reside in each individual of the human race and on account of which it comes about that they die; but he sets out a general cause that looks upon all in the genus equally," and so on. He speaks just as if hereditary corruption were not a general cause looking upon all men equally — when yet that is as common as the death of those who have sinned is common, as human nature is common to them, indeed as imputation is said to be common. So little by little the doctrine of the force and guilt of hereditary corruption, which the first reformers defended with highest zeal, is neglected and nearly blotted out, that it may give place to that imputation which those great men either altogether did not know, or even refuted.
52: "Nor is it fair," he adds, "that we should say that cause is remote and far off, because here one must look not to spaces of years and ages, but to the efficacy of the thing." What? is an injustice that did not stick in me, but in Adam alone, dead some thousands of years before I existed, a cause equally immediate and proximate to me or to my death, as that which inheres in me most inwardly and is by the confession of all the cause of my death (Romans 5:12)? Did not corruption also follow Adam's sin, and death this? corruption is therefore a nearer cause of death than the sin that stuck in Adam alone. "Nor indeed," he subjoins, "do those who say corruption is derived from Adam propose Adam on that account as a remote and distant cause of that corruption — namely, because there is for us with him a most near union by reason of blood, though not by reason of person." On the contrary they propose him as a remote and distant cause of that corruption — that is, the first, from which it flowed out to all others. Therefore that blood is here distinguished from person, and that by reason of the former, not of the latter, a most near union with Adam is said to be ours — that for my part I do not understand. For my blood differs from blood, and my nature from nature, as much as person from Adam's person: the difference of each alike is numerical, not specific. And as I drew my person, so also my nature, through all my intermediate parents from Adam. For Adam is our father not nearest but first; and I have received, or could receive, nothing from him except through my nearest parents.
53: "But," he says, "since a comparison is here instituted between Christ and Adam, the disobedience committed by Adam is no more to be called a remote cause of our condemnation than the obedience performed by Christ is to be called a remote cause of our justification." As if a comparison could not be instituted between two causes of opposite effects, when they are first in their kind, unless each alike is proximate! Who does not know that Christ's obedience is the adequate and only cause of our justification, but Adam's disobedience only an inadequate and partial cause of our condemnation? for we are condemned not on account of Adam's actual sin alone, but also on account of the hereditary corruption inhering in us, and all our other sins whether actual or habitual; whereas yet we are justified on account of Christ's one obedience, and in no way on account of ours. This cause, therefore, since it is the sole and only cause of justification, is the same both first and proximate; but that, since it is not alone, but together with it there are many other causes of condemnation, is first in such a way that there is no necessity that it be proximate. What? do we not draw sin and, through sin, condemnation from Adam by natural propagation? Did not both the Fathers of old and our first Reformers use to oppose the propagation of sin to Pelagian imitation, with no mention made of imputation? And yet of natural propagation, in its own kind indeed, Adam is the first cause, but of each of us the nearest or immediate cause he certainly is not. Here therefore the greatest difference is seen between Adam and Christ. Adam is the most remote cause of our generation, whereas Christ is the proximate cause of our regeneration. We are sons of Adam not nearest but remote: for between us and Adam many others are interposed; but we are nearest sons of Christ, as many as believe in him. For by faith we are united to Christ straight and immediately, and also by his Spirit, who, since he is only one in number both in Christ and in all of us, couples us to Christ so immediately that between Christ and the believer there is no middle person. Since the learned man was not ignorant of these things, how could he speak so? "Finally in meritorious causes," he says, "of the kind we are dealing with, there is always proximity, because that merit always acts near (ἐγγύς) and efficaciously." A fine argument! as if efficacy, like cause, could not equally be distinguished into remote and proximate! for each cause has its own force, and when the effect follows, that is efficacy; otherwise it would not be a cause. Did not Adam efficaciously propagate his nature and corruption into us? And yet he is only a remote cause of our nature and corruption. But he himself is not the meritorious cause of our condemnation, but the cause of this cause; for from him flowed the hereditary corruption that is the proximate or immediate cause of our condemnation, and of this the cause was Adam's actual sin. Can we likewise say that Christ's obedience was the cause of some virtue or obedience that is the cause of our justification? To that extent, therefore, there is a memorable difference between Christ's obedience and Adam's disobedience, and the former is to be called the proximate cause of justification, the latter the remote cause of our condemnation (for corruption is interposed). Otherwise how could Adam's actual sin be a meritorious and proximate cause of our condemnation? First, if it is not ours except by imputation, it does not merit our condemnation except by the intervention of imputation. It is therefore not a meritorious cause of our condemnation through itself, but only through an accident, by reason of that imputation, which is a divine action, and so supernatural and voluntary: whereas yet Christ's obedience is a meritorious cause of our justification through itself; namely, performed to that end and counsel by our surety in our place. Which being posited, it follows that our being sinners and being condemned is to be ascribed through itself to that divine action, but to Adam's sin only through an accident — which my conscience in no way suffers me to be led to believe or do. Next, he who imputes sin to some man presupposes that that man exists; he who condemns to death presupposes that he whom he condemns lives. Since therefore of our existing and living, which by nature precedes our condemnation, Adam is only a remote cause, how can he be the proximate cause of our condemnation?
